chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya al-Ash'ari narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Ubayd Allah al-Alawi, from his father, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about the marriage of women given three divorces, and he said to me: 'Your divorce is not permissible for others [to marry them], and their divorce is permissible for you, because you do not consider the three [divorces] to be anything [i.e., one counts as one], while they obligate it [i.e., they consider three to be three].'

key_terms.يُوجِبُونَهَا: They obligate it [consider it binding as three]

ai.seo_question: How does the Shia view of triple divorce differ from other schools regarding remarriage?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* elucidates the principle of *al-gharad* (purpose/intent) in divorce by contrasting the Shia view of three divorces as a single revocable act with the Sunni view of them as three distinct events. Consequently, a woman divorced thrice by Sunnis remains *mahram* to her ex-husband, while one divorced thrice by Shias becomes *halal* for others, highlighting how differing jurisprudential assumptions directly alter marital eligibility.
